speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house seems to have a perfect yen for asking explanations about my humble, unobtrusive bill. If it is not one section asking, it is another section demanding. There have been so many bills reprinted in the last few days, this seems to be a sort of legislative Easter. This bill is the resurrected body of Bill No. 38, iwhich was crucified three days ago by the application of a fifteen-year-old rule for which there did not seem to be very much precedent. It now comes before us clothed with explanations, as with a garment, like some beautiful and ostensibly repentant Magdalen knocking at the doors of society for reentry. I hope it will be received with that kindly interest that society always does accord to people with a lurid past when they are fair to look upon and when their sins are sickbed o'er with the pale cast of repentance.
The bill is exactly the same as the one introduced on March 9; the two are identical, word for word, with the exception that the date is different. On an attached sheet, but

River St. Lawrence ship channel-contract dredging in the St. Lawrence river and Montreal harbour, and the extension of existing weirs, including cost of administration-capital, $2,933,400.

I believe the minister had begun the other evening to give an explanation of the disposal of the St. Lawrence dredging fleet. Before we proceed further perhaps he would like to resume what he was saying on that occasion.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was speaking at the close the other evening. He called it eleven o'clock. Perhaps he would like to continue.

Shortly before eleven o'clock I had just begun to point out that three of the contentions advanced by the minister were not, in my opinion, quite accurate. In the first place he told us that the government began to give out contracts for the dredging of the St. Lawrence in 1929 because it realized the necessity of hurrying the work in order to provide a thirty-five foot channel. The records show that contracts were given quite a few years before 1929, but what strikes me as most peculiar is the information brought down by the minister in which he states:
The number of dredges employed by the contractors and by the department on the St. Lawrence work has varied from time to time and it has happened that work has been done by contractors' dredges when departmental dredges were not fully employed. This has been due in part to the urgency of the work.
(Mr. Neill.]
If the work was really so urgent, why were the government dredges doing nothing when contracts were given out to contractors?
The second point which the minister discussed the other day was the Sorel shipyard. He told us that the Sorel shipyards, to use his own words, were maintained simply to repair the government dredging fleet; that that was the yard's main work. I do not think that is quite an accurate picture. It would lead us to believe that the Sorel shipyard was nothing but a repair yard. That is not so. I said the other day, and I repeat it, that the Sorel shipyard was equipped to do a great deal more than mere repair work; it was equipped not only to repair but to build vessels. In proof of that I would point to the number of vessels that were being built in certain years. For example in 1925 two vessels were building; in 1926, eight; in 1927, twelve; in 1928, ten, and so on. So to say that the Sorel shipyard was simply a small affair without much equipment is far from accurate. The Sorel shipyard was equipped not only to build vessels, but even to manufacture the marine boilers required therefor. Furthermore the number of employees at the yard goes to show that it could not have been a small establishment. The minister stated the other day that at times there were between nine hundred and one thousand men employed, so certainly the capacity was much greater than the minister indicated.
But the most important aspect of this deal is the question of valuation. The minister told us the other night that he had asked a private company, the Canadian Appraisal Company, to make a survey of the equipment which was to be sold, and that he based his calculations upon such survey. I believe if we studied the story of the valuation we should find that there is a great deal more to be said than just what the minister told us the other day. For example I have in my hand a part of the return brought down by the minister, showing on page 9 a summary of appraisal values by the Canadian Appraisal Company. I should like to discuss item No. 1, which reads as follows:
Land, including wharves, railway sidings, paving, fences and drainage, value, $60,000.
I believe that valuation is entirely wrong, and I propose to give figures taken from the department's own records to show what the government paid for the land in the first place, proving positively that the valuation of $60,000 is a ridiculous figure in the face of what it cost the government.
On May 26, 1932, the following purchases were made at Sorel: parcel 442, 4,356 square

Supply-Transport-St. Lawrence Dredging
feet; parcel 443, 4,356 square feet; parcel 444, 17,424 square feet; parcel 445, 15,130 square feet; a total area at that time of 51,266 square feet were purchased. The purchase price was $18,316.62, which means roughly 35 cents per square foot. I refer not to the buildings or improvements but to the actual land itself, upon which there can be no such thing as depreciation. This deal was made in 1932 at the lowest point of the depression, and one has only to read the speeches of the then leader of the opposition to know what the condition of the country was at that time and how low values were. Therefore that price of 35 cents a square foot was paid by the department at a time when values were at the lowest possible level.
What land is it that the hon. member is referring to? Where is it located?
I have given the minister the parcel numbers.
Is it part of the shipyard property?
Yes, I believe it is now.
The hon. member does not know whether it is or not.

It is land that is now part of the shipyard property, commercial land used for that kind of purpose in the town of Sorel. Since the shipyard property is in a much more valuable location, I imagine it would be more valuable than other property.
Downtown property in the town of Sorel?

The situation at Sorel is this. The Richelieu river runs into the St. Lawrence there, and the best possible industrial locations would be immediately at the junction of the two rivers. That means that there is water frontage on two sides, an ideal condition for property for that purpose. In any event these are prices paid by the department for land there, and I take these parcels as examples because they were purchased in 1932 at a time when values were known to be low.

My hon. friend stated that this land was purchased by the government and later sold, and he has just told us something which would indicate that nothing of the kind took place. Suppose he apologize to the committee for giving false information.
I do not believe I have given false information. What I am trying to do is to establish the value.
Did the hon. member say, or did he not, that the land was purchased and then sold?
Let me put it this way. I am establishing the value of land around that point.
Let us have this straight. The hon. member either can or cannot tell the truth, and we want to know.
Order.
Is this land that was bought and later sold, or not?

If the minister is incensed now he had better reserve his comments until later, because this is just the beginning. What I am trying to do is to establish the value of land in that particular location, and I am taking the year 1932 when this deal was made in order to have the lowest possible valuation that can be made.
Is this land in the town of Sorel?
I have given the locations.
It is part of the town of Sorel?
I believe that parcels 442, 443, 444 and 445 are either in St. Joseph de Sorel or in Sorel.
Which town is the shipyard in?
It is in St. Joseph de Sorel.
And not the town of Sorel?
It is across the Richelieu river from the city of Sorel.
But not in the town of Sorel; in other words it is in the parish of St. Joseph?
Possibly so; it is across the river.

So the hon. member quoted a number of assessments on property in the town of Sorel the other day just for window dressing, is that it? They had nothing to do with the shipyard, because the shipyard is not in the town of Sorel. Is that the idea?

How can the minister get away from this explanation? This is the value of industrial land in that part of the country. If he figures that the government paid too much at 35 cents a square foot I am willing to take a much lower figure, and I can still show the minister a great discrepancy between the $60,000 the Canadian Appraisal Company said it was worth and the true value. So, continuing with these figures, we find that the land eventually sold was not a matter of simply a few hundred thousand

speechtext:
My hon. friend again

The trouble with that is with regard to one figure; something over twenty-four acres are shown without any value at all. They appear as a gift from some other department, so it is impossible to establish the true cost to the government. Furthermore, how else can we ascertain the value if we do not take into consideration the value of properties adjacent to the property we wish to sell? You must have some basis of valuation, and here I am taking land which the government itself purchased at 35 cents per square foot. If that figure is too high I can put it at 25 cents and still show a discrepancy.
In passing I should like to point out that this $60,000 was not the actual amount realized by the Canadian government from the sale of this property. In reality the amount realized was only 80 per cent of that figure, so actually this land brought a return of some $48,000, when it was worth at least $500,000.
Let me go further with these values. We could group together several items. Let us take items 1 and 2, which are valued in the report of the appraisal company at $60,000 and $129,789 respectively, making a total of $189,789. Item No. 1 covers wharves, railway sidings, paving, fences and drainage, while No. 2 covers other properties. As was mentioned the other day, the assessment roll of the city of Sorel values the government property at more than a million dollars. The minister may claim that the shipyard is located in St. Joseph de Sorel-and that some of it remains unsold and

is still in the possession of the government. I am prepared to take the minister's explanation in that regard, and it is possible that the valuation covers more property than was sold. Nevertheless I believe I have shown that the valuation of that particular land is not at all fair, and that it has resulted in quite a serious loss to the Canadian government.
We might go further and take up the question of the equipment itself. The instructions from the minister to the appraisal company were that a fair valuation was to be placed upon this equipment. Let us turn to item No. 10, which includes the dredging fleet at Sorel and Quebec. The valuation shown by the Canadian Appraisal Company is $1,534,750, and of that amount eighty per cent was received as the sale price, that is to say $1,227,800. Now let us compare that price with the cost to this government of some of that equipment. It may be all right to tell us that this equipment was absolutely obsolete, but I am not going to deal with any obsolete equipment. I am going to mention two pieces of that equipment which together cost the Canadian government more than was realized from the sale of all this equipment to this private firm. We have dredge No. 16, built in 1923, and dredge No. 17, built in 1931. These two dredges alone cost more than the total amount realized by the government from the sale of all the equipment. Dredge No. 16 cost $837,200 and dredge No. 17 cost $444,535, or a total cost to the Canadian government of $1,281,735.

Is the hon. member
able to give to the committee the proper depreciation from year to year on equipment of that kind?

Well, Mr. Chairman,
even if these two dredges depreciated to such an extent that they vanished, still there would be the rest of the equipment to take into consideration. Perhaps it is necessary to read the list of equipment and show the cost prices. Here we have dredge No. 3, at south channel; value for scrap, $7,500. Then there is dredge No. 4, also valued at $7,500, which originally cost the government $94,564. This was an old dredge, and it may be that this value is approximately correct. Dredge No. 5, built in 1927, was valued at $70,000 and cost the Canadian government $388,952. Dredge No. 8, built in 1907, cost the government $450,435 and was valued at $150,000. It is worthy of note that this dredge was rebuilt in 1928 and changed to a bucket dredge, so that the original cost would have to be increased to

the extent of about $150,000. Then there were dredges Nos. 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17, and No. 18 which is not yet finished. There was also Churchill No. 1, built in 1928. There were also several tugs; in fact in all, apart from the two pieces I have mentioned as costing the Canadian government more than the total amount realized for the equipment, we find that there were included fifty-nine other pieces of floating equipment which so far have not been mentioned.
When we find that these two dredges alone cost that amount of money, what are we to say? Has the depreciation on this equipment been so heavy that they might be said to have vanished into thin air? When it comes to the matter of depreciation I should like to relate the stoiy of one particular dredge, which will indicate that this equipment was still capable of doing work for some considera-able time. It must not be thought that a dredge which cost the taxpayers of this country some $444,000 in 1931 would become scrap in 1937. I do not believe that that is possible, no matter how much work it has done. If, then, these figures are not satisfactory to the minister and do not indicate to him that the appraisal of the Canadian Appraisal Company was certainly not in accordance with the valuation placed upon the property, let me return to the auditor general's report.
The other day the Minister of Finance mentioned that the auditor general always gave us accurate figures. I believe he does, when he gets them. But there are times when he does not get them, and that is what I meant the other day. The Minister of Transport has not yet given us a satisfactory explanation as to why no inventory was made prior to 1936. It is true that the minister has not always had this particular branch under his administration; I know, for example, that this matter was given to the minister only within the last few years. He could not possibly have known what had been going on in the past, and the remarks I have just addressed to him to-day are remarks which really should be for those who administered this department before he became its head. However, he must now be in a position to provide us with a satisfactory answer.
I did mention the auditor general's report; apparently it is found that there might have been some misunderstanding about it, so I have brought with me to-day the auditor general's instructions concerning values. It was maintained that these were original values, without any depreciation having been placed upon them. That is not so. I say that simply because the first inventory was
made in 1936; it appears in the report of the auditor general for the first time in that year. Four months later the dredging fleet was sold. There could not have been any change in those four months; at least there could not have been depreciation to warrant anything like the depreciation claimed. What are the instructions of the auditor general? Let us go over them:
In either case the inventory should be prepared to show the total value of such property on hand.
Then he tells us how to arrive at that value. Then, in regard to values-
I wish to point out that as the principle of depreciation is not being observed-
Mark this,
-under the policy of the government respecting the value of public property in general, it is not intended that depreciation should be considered. It is suggested therefore that property values once established-
And this is my point-property values "once established" for the first time; and they were established in the report of the auditor general under date of December 31, 1936. In this particular case they had not been established before, because no inventory was ever supplied to the auditor general. Therefore the values once established were the values established on December 31, 1936, as instructed by the auditor general. He says:
-either on a cost or an estimated basis, should be maintained unchanged in your records from year to year until such property is finally disposed of-
In this particular case the property was disposed of only four months after the valuation took place. So that it cannot be said the minister-

Yes. The position is this: These values were fixed for the first time on December 31, 1936.

I would simply draw the minister's attention to this point, that I gave him the page and volume number of the auditor general's report-page 240, volume I, 1929. It is a public record, filed in this House of Commons. I have stated just where the quotation is. What more can I do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member can then proceed to quote it correctly.
I am doing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member quotes it, he must quote it.

All these matters are of public record, and the minister can read it for himself. But the conclusion I am drawing is this, that no tenders were called for, and the reason given was that it was adjudged to be a matter of public expediency. Yet we find that negotiations had been going on since 1927 -for the building of such a boat, and then finally it was said that the matter had become so urgent that it was necessary to build the boat without calling for tenders.
To go back again into the days gone by-this concerns the money of the taxpayers of this

country-let us look at some of the contracts which have been made in the past. The minister stated the other day that the principle of giving contracts was started in 1929. I do not believe that that is an accurate statement of the case, because contracts were given long before 1929.
Take contract No. 15423, which was awarded to Les Chantiers Manseau of Sorel, Quebec. This company later became the Marine Industries Limited, with yards at Sorel, and their equipment there. Then take contract No. 15493.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, while I do not desire to interrupt my hon. friend, I think I am right in stating that he has now spoken considerably more than forty minutes. Would it not facilitate the proceedings if he were to confine his remarks to that point? He will have the right to speak again, but if he wishes to proceed now at any length unanimous consent will be necessary. I have no objection to the hon. member proceeding, but I raise the point just that we may keep in order.
I have been interrupted by the minister. He has just sat down, and had quite a number of words to say.
You do not get another forty minutes now because of that.
I was interrupted two or three times, and I sat down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule as to the forty-minute limit is the same in committee as when the Speaker is in the chair, and unless an hon. member has the unanimous consent of the house he must take his seat when his forty minutes have expired.
I think, Mr. Chairman, you ought to take into consideration the fact that the Minister of Transport interrupted and made a statement during my forty minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired, and I must ask him to resume his seat.
Does not the interruption of the Minister of Finance-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Interruptions do not affect the rule.

On several occasions it was more than a mere interruption, and two or three have spoken during the hon. member's time. I submit that according to a strict interpretation of the rule the member who is speaking has had a chance to come to his feet again, and he is on his feet again after a speech by the Minister of Finance, and therefore is due for forty minutes more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On that point of order, Mr. Chairman, whether an interruption entitles the member who has the floor to another forty minutes from the time of the interruption, I would submit as one who has suffered from interruptions quite a good deal and never been allowed for them in that manner-although I have had to acknowledge the courtesy and consideration of the house in granting me more than my original forty minutes-that we would be establishing a new rule if we said that interruptions such as have just taken place entitle a speaker to an additional forty minutes. I have no objection as a member to allowing my hon. friend to finish his speech. I merely rose to call attention to the fact that he had already exceeded by more than five minutes his forty minutes, and I think five minutes would probably be sufficient to allow for the interruptions. But we should be establishing, I believe, a new rule, Mr. Chairman, if we said that interruptions, or points of order raised, automatically give the member who has the floor an additional forty minutes from the time of the interruption.
I admit that, but I would consider the minister's statement a little more than an interruption.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member wishes the indulgence of the committee, I am entirely in favour of giving him more time if he is going to speak to the item. At the moment we are discussing an item of the Department of Transport, which previously was the Department of Marine, with reference to St. Lawrence dredging and the Sorel shipyard. When my hon. friend was interrupted last he was talking about dredging under the Public Works department, which has nothing to do with this item at all.

That is drawing it too fine, because since I have been here nearly every member has violated almost every rule of the house.

If there are rules, we should respect them, and there is a rule confining a member to forty minutes. But if the hon. member wishes to discuss this particular item,
I shall be delighted to ask for unanimous consent to permit him to continue for a reasonable time.

There are occasions upon which the enforcement of rules is dangerous to all concerned, and I think in this particular instance, because of the interpretation that might be placed upon any curtailment of the discussion at the present time, we would be well advised and it would be in the interests of the house generally to let the hon. member proceed. So if any hon. member feels that anyone may be left besmirched by cutting the hon. member off, he can dismiss that from his mind at once. Let the hon. member proceed.
That was the point I had in mind. I think it would be well to let him go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member has the indulgence of the committee to speak for more than forty minutes, should he not at least respect the other rule and confine himself to the item before the committee? He should not, if he is given the indulgence of the committee on a particular point, undertake a roving commission over everything; because obviously the minister cannot answer with respect to matters extraneous to his department.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In order to clarify the whole situation, I would point out to the hon. member that while, with the consent of the committee, he may continue, he must confine his remarks to the item under discussion.

The item under discussion represents almost $3,000,000, Which sum will be paid to a private company to dredge the St. Lawrence, and the dredging becomes necessary because equipment owned by the government has been disposed of. This was formerly under the Public Works department, and has now been taken over by the Department of Transport.
It was never under the Department of Public Works; it was under the Department of Marine.

The minister is drawing fine distinctions. At any rate it was under a different minister. It is necessary when we review the situation to go back some time in the past. What I am emphasizing is this. I regret that the impression should prevail among the public that because a utility is publicly owned it is necessarily badly administered. Private enterprise on all sides points to examples of public administration which it is said have not been successful, and that is used as an argument against public ownership of various utilities. If in our public administration there are departments that are not administered as efficiently as they should be, that makes it possible for private interests to argue against public ownership. They say, " When that happens under government administration, what is to be expected "?
The point I wish to bring out is that work on various contracts was begun days, and in some instances weeks, before the contract was signed. Does that mean that any individual company can plant its equipment in the St. Lawrence and start dredging and then come to the government and get a contract? I do not understand how it is that any contractor can begin work before his contract is signed. Possibly there is a logical explanation, and, as the minister has said, he will be in a position shortly to explain to the committee how things of this sort come about.
We have been talking about values, and in my opinion that is relevant to the item before the committee. The minister made it clear to me that he wanted a complete statement with regard to values and therefore he must be interested in the subject from that point of view. Why not tell the story of the famous dredge Marine and Fisheries No. 10, which is now known as Manseau 101, or of Marine and Fisheries No. 11, which is now known as Manseau 103? Both were built a long time ago. They were owned by the government and then sold after a certain period.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How long ago?

I do not know exactly. At any rate they were disposed of to a private individual in Montreal. They became the property of Manseau Shipyards Limited, and to-day one of these dredges is doing contract work.
On the order paper there appears a question of mine with regard to painting and repairs to

Supply-Transport-St. Lawrence Dredging
the buildings at the Sorel shipyards. The question is No. 7 on to-day's order paper and part 2 reads:
How much money was spent for painting and repair to the buildings at the Sorel shipyards for the five months preceding July 22nd, 1937?
That was the date on which the Sorel shipyards were sold. I have not received the answer. The question was first asked on May 4, and it is now May 13. Possibly the minister has not yet had time to secure the information.

The information has just
come to hand and I shall be glad to give the answers orally. The first question is:
Did the government sell coal barge No. 6 to the General Dredging Company last year?
The answer is, yes.
If so, (a) has the government used or rented coal barge No. 6 from the General Dredging Company since it was sold to them?
The answer is, yes.
(b)	how much rent has the government paid each day?
The answer is that the contract was for S265 per day for a period not exceeding ten days.
(c)	for what purpose was it used?
For the purpose of assisting in the spring rush of laying buoys at the Montreal agency.
2.	How much money was spent for painting and repair to the buildings at the Sorel shipyards for the five months preceding July 22, 1937?
The answer is $2,058.96.

I am glad to get the
information. I realize that the minister did not have very much time in which to get it. If I understand rightly, the barge was rented for a period of ten days at $265 per day. Is that correct?
Yes.

When the shoe is on
the other foot what happens? When the government rented to a private contractor certain equipment at least comparable to this they rented it at $100 a month. Rock crusher No 1 was taken from the Sorel shipyards in 1931 and has been rented at $100 a month. It is now the property of the company who rented it, they having bought it for $15,000. But when the government want to rent equipment from a private concern they have to pay $265 a day. If they paid only half or only a quarter of that sum, compare the rent paid by the government with the rent paid by a private concern to
the government. As I say, the government for a whole month received $100 for a rock crusher which is now in the yards at Sorel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman expect to rent an automobile at the same rate as a bicycle?

If the Minister of
Finance would visit the shipyards at Sorel he would see the sort of work the rock breaker does. It is used for breaking rock at the bottom of the channel, and is considerably larger than any automobile. An automobile would cost to rent $50 a month. He knows that this sort of discrimination cannot be defended.
The figures I have used to-day in connection with this item were supplied by various government departments. I realize my limitations. I know my capacities, and it is not possible for me to delve into this matter as deeply as someone with better qualifications might. I do not think it is an easy task for one person without proper information to get at all the facts. I rely upon the Minister of Transport and I know that he will be able to explain to us why no inventory was taken before December 31, 1936. I hope he will explain that and other matters that I have brought to his attention. I could have read more of the contracts and shown the discrepancy between the date the contract was awarded and1 the date the work began, but I leave that off the record. My purpose is this: I believe that certain functions performed by a government should be performed as efficiently as they could be performed Iby any private enterprise. I believe if this kind of government administration is permitted-loose accounting, for example, or careless accounting-it gives ground for private industry to say: "See what happens when a thing is owned by the government. This is what you get under public ownership when governments are administering anything." I believe that if the facts are told it would be possible for any department of the government to administer any business in this country properly, and do it as efficiently as private enterprise ever can. I pause, because I believe that my time has expired once more: I shall probably resume later.

It is difficult to grasp the idea that the hon. member is trying to convey, but in. summary is it this: that the government has been selling machinery to private companies at ten to twenty cents on the dollar, and then giving them large contracts in which they use this very machinery and

I s.m not a lawyer, but if I were I would say that that is a very leading question. I do not know what interpretation the government can place upon it; I have simply attempted to put on record the facts.
I am not defending the government; I say if that is the purpose of it they should answer.

I agree that possibly the government will answer, and I should like the hon. member to join with me in insisting that it should be done. The minister no doubt has a few remarks to make, and perhaps he would care to make them now.

I have listened for the last hour and a half or thereabouts to some very serious accusations. If any part of them were true, I would have no option but to resign from the government and place my seat at the disposal of my electors. Fortunately none of them are true in any particular, therefore I shall stay here.
Now I should be feeling very serious resentment, for as I stated clearly in the committee, I personally attended to every detail of the negotiations for the sale of this equipment. Therefore the accusation is against my personal honesty, and I should feel very bitter against the hon. member. But as a matter of fact I cannot bring myself to feel so at all.
You should sympathize with him.

I realize that the hon. member is very young and very gullible. Months ago we heard rumours that a great scandal was to break in the house about the sale of this Sorel shipyard, something that would shake the government. Then an obscure journal published in Quebec began to say that it was expected that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Pelletier) would make the presentation. We then had the hon. member visiting Sorel. He was taken to the assessor's office, not of the village of St. Joseph de Sorel but of the town of Sorel. He was furnished with a list of assessments in the town of Sorel, which he solemnly read to us here a while ago, I presume to lead the committee to the conclusion that these were assessments of shipyard property.

Who took him to
Sorel?

We all know who took him
to Sorel.
Tell us.

I simply want to explain
why I feel no great bitterness in the matter. The men who had been advertising this situation in advance needed not only someone young and very gullible, but someone completely addled as to financial affairs, because without that it would have been impossible to show to any hon. member the documents he was shown, and expect that hon. member to accept them seriously. This is all the more the situation since my own department has answered clearly and fully every question that he asked, and the hon. member has in his possession absolutely correct statements of everything that he has given in a garbled and distorted manner to this committee.
Let us start at the beginning. Let us take his statement about assessments of property at Sorel. He tried, I think, in his speech a week ago to lead the committee to the conclusion that the land comprising the Sorel shipyard was worth a million dollars, and was carried on assessment rolls of the town of Sorel at that price. Of course at that time he did not explain to the committee, as he has admitted to-day, that the shipyard is not in the town of Sorel but in the parish of St. Joseph de Sorel.

Now what do we conclude from that? The government owns in St. Joseph de Sorel 3,940,000 square feet of land, which is of course the old ordnance property and the shipyard. The shipyard represents 800,000 square feet, or a little more than one-fifth of the whole. If my hon. friend had gone to the proper town for his tax appraisal he would have found that the appraised value on the books of the town is a little over $100,000, we will say at the outside $125,000, for the shipyard property and the land that was sold. It now stands in the books of the town with an assessment of $150,000 against the new owners. So much for the appraisal of the land.
Now let us come to the auditor general's inventory, which is simply a statement carried in the books of the government showing what
various properties cost. There may be some obligation on departments to keep those inventories more or less up to date, and I may say that the rules of the auditor general provide that items shall be entered in the inventory at cost. They are carried at cost until the items are actually disposed of by the government, and of course, some items are never disposed of, so as a result the "inventory" is a more or less meaningless affair. However, the auditor general did call to my attention the fact that our inventory was not up to date, and I issued instructions that it be brought up to date. I have in my hand a copy of the document furnished the auditor general by our department, giving the items in detail. This was furnished in response to his request and is the document from which the figures quoted by my hon. friend were taken. In this list there are two columns, the first showing the original cost of the article and the second the market value, as it is described here, as in 1936. The figures given to my hon. friend were the cost figures.
What was the date of that document?

February, 1937. It is the inventory of the fleet at the end of 1936, the first inventory of that equipment we ever supplied to the auditor general. This inventory adds up to $7,872,007.01, which is the figure my hon. friend gave.

The minister stated
there was no inventory supplied before. Will he please explain why?

I cannot say that; all I know is that the first request came to me, as mim< ister, in 1936, and I complied with it. 1 thought if the auditor general wanted the inventory he had better have it, and I issued instructions to have it made up and given to him. That was the first request I ever received, and I complied with it as soon as the inventory could be made up.
The figure given by my hon. friend as being the original cost of this equipment was $7,872,007.01. I have the present day value, which was furnished to the auditor general at the same time, and that figure is $1,953,900. However, on this list there are many items that were not sold. For instance, we have the steamship Bellechasse, the steamship Berthier, the steamship Detector, the steamship Frontenac, the tug Lanoraie, the tug Laviolette, and the tug Lavaltrie, which the government still own. The minister is telling us now of the equipment he still has on hand.
I did not mention anything about the equip- ' ment that remained unsold. The figures I quoted covered the list supplied to me by the department, and had nothing to do with the equipment remaining unsold. I do not know anything about that.
My hon. friend quoted the list furnished him by the department, I take it?
That is right.

I have shown how all that figures out. I think I stated that it was because my hon. friend is absolutely addled as a financier that he has been chosen for this work. I cannot state the position more clearly than I have.

I will put it this way-the person who chose you to take on the work.

I was not chosen. I am doing it of my own accord because it is in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer and the truth.
It must have brought you in rontact with very strange friends, then.

I did not say anybody hired him.

No, I deny that. No insinuation of the kind was made, and I think no hon. member could reasonably take that from what I said. I did not say he was hired for the work.

How, actually, is the

The selection is made entirely by the board of railway commissioners, who administer this fund. The department has nothing to do with the selection. The board hears applications for the abolition of grade crossings in the order, I suppose, in which they are filed, determines the merits of the application, whether there should be a division of the cost, and if so, what it should be, and then issues its order. Will the most dangerous crossings be eliminated first? Is there a plan working to that end?

The board does not initiate
grade crossing projects, but simply passes upon applications made. As a matter of fact there is no great rush of applications to the board, strange as that may seem. If it were a very dangerous crossing would the board wait for an application, or would they use their own judgment to eliminate it?

The board does not initiate
any projects; application must be made.

Who has control in a situation such as I will now describe? Somewhere close to the city of Grand Forks the railway passes over the main automobile road and there is a bridge constructed of stone and brick, I believe. This is an item in which the western members are very much interested. I note that there is an increase in this vote. What is the total cost of operation and maintenance, and the total revenue? I trust the government are giving due consideration to that port. It is a very important port, and I have talked with different men interested in shipping who claim that for a considerable part of the year it is as safe as the St.

Lawrence waterways. I trust the government are not slackening in their efforts to make it a success. What effort is the government making to get business for that port?

The vote under consideration is for the Hudson Bay railway. I assume my hon. friend refers to a later vote for the port of Churchill. For the railway the cost of operation last year was $364,000, and of maintenance, $336,500, making a total of $700,500. The operating revenues were $364,000, leaving an estimated deficit of $336,500.
This year we are providing for operating expenses, $329,000 and maintenance, $370,000, or a total of $699,000. and we anticipate an operating revenue of $329,000 and are providing for a deficit of $370,000.

How many vessels came
into that port during last year?

There were two cargoes
shipped out last year. There was one in and there were two out.

What would the cargoes
consist of?

The incoming cargo was general merchandise. The boat is put on the berth at London for all goods offering for movement into western Canada by Churchill. It takes general merchandise, hardware, fencing, glass, binder twine, material of that kind.
The outgoing cargoes were what?
Entirely wheat.

As this Hudson Bay railway and the port are more or less the baby of the Minister of Finance, I trust the government are making every effort to make that port a success. I think if a little more advertising were done and effort made to get business, it might be put on a paying basis. If they could get another $370,000 worth, it would practically carry its operating expenses.

Last year, as my hon. friend knows, was a very exceptional year in grain traffic. There was a premium for cash wheat over the option as high as twenty-five and thirty cents, and naturally wheat at Churchill is not cash wheat. So market conditions put Churchill out of line last year. For a time Vancouver was in almost the same position. Some years ports have a good flow of the grain, and in others they do not. We did everything possible to attract grain to Churchill last year, but the best position we
could find would have required a cash contribution from the government of about eight cents a bushel to justify the movement of grain to Churchill.
Are the expenses of the operation of the elevator included in this?
No; this is just the railway. The port is another item; we shall come to it later.

V hat passenger and freight service is given on this railway? Would the minister give a short review of the present situation, the land of traffic that is carried, whether it is operated all winter, and other details?

In the summer months the train runs every second day between The Pas and Churchill. It is a mixed train, a way freight with passenger accommodation. That train leaves The Pas one day and comes back the next. Of course, when grain is moving, additional freights are put on as required. In the winter the service is cut down to one trip a month through to Churchill, but there is a weekly service between Gillam and The Pas. Gillam is about three hundred miles from The Pas.
Is there any increase in the freight traffic, or are any mines being opened up along the railway?

As my hon. friend knows,
the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company's mine at Flinflon is tributary to this line, as is also the Sherritt-Gordon mine. We have heavy traffic over the part near The Pas from these mines. Unfortunately no further worthwhile mining development has been discovered along the line.
Before the item passes perhaps I may be permitted to say a word or two, because this railway is in the constituency I represent in this house.

It is your baby just
now.

Yes, and I am rather proud of the baby. The Minister of Transport has mentioned the mining development in northern Manitoba. It may be of interest to the committee to learn that to-day there are five operating mines in Manitoba north of the town of The Pas, four in the western part of the province and one in the eastern part. Seventy miles from The Pas, at Flinflon, is the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company operation, which gives steady employment to 1,700 men, and produces copper, zinc,

gold, silver and some other rare metals. Eighty miles north of The Pas is the jumping-off place for another mine which came into operation two years ago and to-day gives steady employment, as I recall, to something like 150 men. Then, still further north, about 250 miles, is a point called Ilford, from which all the freight goes into the God's Lake mine in eastern Manitoba, and another development that is taking place east of that again in the province of Ontario at a place called Sachego lake.

Would the minister say
how many miles up the railway it is to that connection for God's lake?

It is at a place called
Ilford. I am not sure of the distance, but my recollection is that it is about 250 miles.
Long before the crossing of the river?

Yes, before we came to
the Nelson river. At the moment this is really a pioneer road. I have not the slightest doubt that if it had not been for the last eight years of depression the progress in northern Manitoba, as indeed in the northern parts of our other provinces, would have been very much greater than it has been. Undoubtedly, in this northern country, in Manitoba as well as in the other provinces, there are all the evidences of rich mineral possibilities. While I am aware of the popular notion held in eastern Canada with regard to the Hudson Bay railway; while I am awrare of the fact that some people fairly high in authority have condemned it, nevertheless I venture to say that the time will come when the Hudson Bay railway will justify its construction and operation just as much as the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway has justified its construction and operation in the province of Ontario. Even in my brief memory I can recall that when the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario was built there was a great deal of opposition to the spending of money to build a road into a wilderness that would never produce anything. Well, development has entirely belied those statements, and I am equally certain that the same thing will hold true of the Hudson Bay railway.
I might just add this, that I think Canadians generally fail to appreciate the possibilities of' the development of wealth in our northern areas. Certainly one of the essentials for that development is transportation. While it is true that we have been obliged to provide sums of money to make up deficits resulting from the operation of this
TMr. Crerar.]
road, I am quite certain that the day will come w'hen these deficits will cease and the developments along the road will be making a worthwhile contribution to the wealth of this country. It was unfortunate that, because of conditions in the west last year, no grain went to Churchill. Undoubtedly Churchill will ship grain; but last year Saskatchewan produced scarcely enough wheat for its own bread and seed, and under those conditions no grain was available to go to Churchill. My colleague the Minister of Transport referred to the market conditions that obtained during practically the whole season. Because of the scarcity of our hard wheat on the prairies, the cash premiums on spot grain went to as high as twenty-five or thirty cents a bushel over the future months. Consequently grain could not be sent to Churchill, or rather it could be sent there, but no dealer or trader would take the risk of purchasing it under these high premiums unless he was sure he could move it out to take advantage of the market at any moment.
The minister still thinks it is a practicable route for the future?

I have never had any doubt of that, and I have never been more certain of it than I am at this time. That route will develop. The time will come when it will be one of the important trade and development routes of Canada. It may not be in our day, but that time will come. I am satisfied that in regard to northern Manitoba and the Hudson Bay railway we shall have a repetition of the very fine contribution that has been made by the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway to the development of northern Ontario.
I just wished to say this word in justification of this vote, because I would not want hon. members to continue in the view-if they hold it-that is held by some of our friends and critics in eastern Canada, that the Hudson Bay railway is simply a great sink-hole which never should have been built. It is a development road. The criticism may be made that it was built a little ahead of time. I do not think so. Certainly, if that road had not been built to The Pas and had not been extended further, we would not have had the great mining development that has taken place even in Manitoba within the last ten years. I am sure hon. members will agree that if this country needs anything to-day, it needs development of our hidden wealth, because only in that way can we reach a national income which will enable us to carry the

burdens that have been placed not only upon the federal government but upon provincial governments as well.

I heartily agree with everything that has been said by the Minister of Mines and Resources with regard to the importance of developing our northern country. The Minister of Transport has stated that there is only one train a month into Churchill during the winter. Is there any air service? If not, it does seem to me that those people should be given better service than one train a month.

There is one train a month to Churchill from The Pas, it is true, but there is a regular service every week to a point something beyond mile 300, which serves the intermediate country. The monthly service to Churchill is sufficient to meet the needs of the town during those months of the year when the port is icebound. The weekly service supplies the mining areas on either side of the road that I mentioned a little earlier.
What is the population of the port during the closed season?
It depends upon the volume of trade.
There are about 200 people, including employees of the port, railway men and a few wives.
How many are temporary and how many are permanent employees?
May I remind hon. members that for the moment we are discussing a railway item. When we reach the appropriate vote in the estimates, we shall give the information.

Is the government doing anything to induce or to assist prospectors to get into the area by way of building trails or roads, so that they can get at the mineralized area? H so, what is being done? It is important, so far as the railway is concerned, because we know the railway needs traffic.
I would suggest that if the hon. member wishes to become clear on the point, he should take a trip over the line some time, especially when he talks about trails over the barren lands.
I am asking for information.
The section near Churchill is not a very good prospecting country; we Shall put it in that way.
Then the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Mines and Resources do not agree. There is something wrong there, somewhere.

I dissent from the remark of my colleague the Minister of Transport. There is a lot of very good prospecting territory for several hundred miles north of The Pas; our geological reports so indicate. The same is true of northern Saskatchewan. I would make the statement for the first three hundred or three hundred and fifty miles along the railway, from The Pas, north.
Possibly at this point I should mention another interesting fact. The Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company at Flinflon have invested over 830,000,000 in that north country. They have a power plant on the Churchill river seventy miles north of Flinflon. A year ago they had to add an additional unit to that plant, and this year they are adding another one. I believe they will now reach their maximum development on the Churchill river. On the Nelson river, farther east, several hundred thousand horse power of electrical energy is capable of development.
My point is that the whole area is only in the beginning of its development. With the railway we now have facilities whereby prospectors can get in. With the aid of aeroplanes from The Pas and Flinflon they can cover quite a large area economically. Under the vote for mining roads which has been passed by parliament in each of the last two years, sums of money have been spent on small improvements here and there to reduce costs of transportation. The work may be that of taking rocks out of a stream to permit the passage of a loaded canoe or boat. It may be that of putting in a dam here or there to raise the water and make a stream navigable. It may be the work of clearing ground around a portage, or building short stretches of road. All these improvements cheapen the cost of getting essential materials into the country to help in its development. That procedure has been followed not only in Manitoba but in Ontario and Quebec, and particularly in British Columbia. I would say to the hon. member for Vancouver South that I doubt if there is any province in Canada which has benefited more from those expenditures than has British Columbia. We are trying only to carry along a sensible development. I do not believe I can add anything further; perhaps I have already taken up too much time of the committee.

I suggest to the Minister of Mines and Natural Resources that he might be helped a great deal in the development of northern Manitoba if he borrowed the official railway car of the Minister of Transport and took that minister for a trip to Churchill in order to convince him with respect to the resources in the territory.
I have already obtained a promise from the Minister of Transport, and I serve notice upon him here that I shall hold him to that promise to go to Churchill this summer.
So that there may be no misunderstanding, I have made more trips over the line from The Pas to Churchill and I have spent more time in Churchill than has any other man in the house.

It would appear from his last statement that the minister must have had something to do with the building of the elevators there, before he joined the government. We must remember that the Minister of Transport is the member for Port Arthur. I do not think we shall find among the electors in that constituency much enthusiasm for the port of Churchill. Possibly the Minister of Mines and Resources was out of order in discussing the item. I must say, however, that he has not given much encouragement with respect to developments or efforts being made to make it a grain port. He has cited the premium on wheat at Fort William. I have no doubt the grain men who have interests at Fort William will never be great boosters for Churchill. I trust, however, that both ministers will set aside their personal interests in their respective constituencies and put forth a greater effort to get grain traffic to the port.

I believe the building of the Hudson Bay railway was just a further example of the faith of our people in the future of Canada. I imagine that the gentlemen who sat in this house in the days when the Canadian Pacific railway was being built from eastern to western Canada, or in the days of early development at Montreal, heard the same questions asked as have been asked today with respect to Churchill and the Hudson Bay railway. It was my privilege to visit Churchill on the first passenger train which went to the port, at a time when the present Minister of Finance was Minister of Railways and the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) was an engineer-
Did he run the locomotive?

He was going to Churchill to lay the foundations for the elevator. That building has been referred to as one of the finest structures of its kind in the world. I have continued to visit Churchill for about two weeks each summer, because I like the place very much. Up to date I believe the railway has justified its existence and all the money which has been invested in it. Hon. members have spoken with respect to the failure of Churchill as a wheat port. I believe if those hon. members would look at the wheat quotations for October wheat in 1936 and 1937, they would find that on the option market alone there was in both years an average spread of about fifteen cents between October and May wheat. Would any one in this chamber who had money to invest, invest it in October wheat and store it at Churchill when May wheat was fifteen cents below the October price? Of course no one would do that, and I say that is the reason why the Churchill elevator has not been used.
If the west has a fair crop this year, it is my opinion that we shall not be able to handle the wheat offered to Churchill. We must have confidence in the future of that port. During a stay at The Pas last fall I got a car one afternoon and drove about fifteen miles up the Carrot river valley in the direction of Nipawin, and while on that trip I was amazed to see the wonderful quality of the land in the valley. I was told that there was a large acreage of land, with rich alluvial deposits, and free from stone, to be settled and developed. I have in mind one farmer about ten miles from The Pas who threshed
5,000	bushels of grain last year. I inquired from a man who had made a trip overland from The Pas to Nipawin, a distance of about 130 miles, and he told me that some day that district would be one of the finest agricultural districts in western Canada. I say to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) that when that day comes, we shall not have anything to worry about as far as the Hudson Bay railway or Churchill is concerned. That railway will be one of the most important lines in Canada.
I agree with what the hon. gentleman is saying.

All that is required is a little more confidence in the future of the country. We should appreciate the agricultural and mining possibilities of that north country. I am convinced that some day there will be half a million people on agricultural land between The Pas and Churchill. Only forty-two miles north east of The Pas I saw as fine vegetables

as could be found anywhere in Canada. Grain ripens in that district, as do pumpkins and tomatoes. They can grow anything that can be grown in the Niagara peninsula, with the exception of peaches and a few things like that. In 1927 The Pas won the district prize for vegetables, competing with the whole province. The future of that country is just as assured as was the future of Montreal seventy-five years ago.
I rose in my place to criticize the government for the smallness of the vote being provided this year for this district. Large expenditures are being made in connection with Montreal and other points along the St. Lawrence river, but the expenditures for this district are quite small. I wonder if they are adequate? I have every confidence in the ability of the minister, and I know he is sympathetic toward the Hudson Bay railway and the port of Churchill. However, I submit that port will not be able to achieve its maximum development without the establishment of a bonded warehouse. A seasonal port like Churchill requires a place where an importer can store his goods until he is ready to distribute them throughout the country. A bonded warehouse does not mean that goods come in free of duty; it simply means that a place is provided in which goods may be stored and the payment of duty and other charges deferred until the goods are distributed. I had hoped that some consideration would have been given to this matter this year. There is a warehouse there at the present time, but it is not large enough. Perhaps a division could be made to provide for bonded facilities, but it would be better to extend the warehouse. An expenditure of 810,000 or $20,000 would permit of a considerable extension of the warehouse to accommodate the binder twine, glass, barbed wire and other commodities that are imported into this country to be used principally in western Canada. I hope serious consideration will be given during the coming year to the establishment of a bonded warehouse at Churchill.

Mr. Chairman, it will be recalled that I had my little say on this matter during the debate on the address. The minister was good enough to state at that time that he would give an outline of the activities of the department in connection with drumming up freight for this route. I remember I read the report of the debate in the papers next morning, and I saw where some one who should have known better referred rather disdainfully to the fact that there had not been a carload of wheat shipped through that port last year. I am sorry to
have to state that there have not been many cars of wheat of last year's growing shipped from Saskatchewan to any other port. We cannot ship what we do not grow. Present prospects would seem to indicate that we shall soon be getting back to normal production.
I do nob want to count chickens before they are hatched, but nature in the form of abundant moisture would seem to be setting the hen for a crop.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) speak so hopefully of this project. Churchill was a good port before Montreal or the St. Lawrence route had been used to any extent. It is true that Jacques Cartier landed at Gaspe four hundred years ago, but it was some time after that before any great amount of traffic was going over the St. Lawrence route. I do not want to be thought to be decrying that route; that is not my intention at all. I am glad to see these dredging expenditures being made, because, with our water disappearing, it is necessary to deepen and widen this route. I hope to see the day when Montreal will be an all year port. Everything would seem to indicate that this may happen. I believe our experts and scientists have the ability to perform a feat of that kind. If this can be done, then the same enterprise can produce relatively the same results for Churchill so far as safe navigation for four months in the year is concerned and possibly more.
I was quite encouraged to-day by hearing what I did hear. I could not hear the minister very well, or the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) or the hon. gentleman in the back benches from a Conservative riding, but I understand there was no disposition to discount the possibilities of the Hudson bay route. Two hundred years ago there was on the Prince of Wales island a fortification stronger than any other in Canada at that time. This had been built by the Hudson's Bay Company, possibly with the assistance of the British government. I nearly lost my political scalp when the matter of this port location was trembling in the balance. Perhaps I would have, if it had not been for the truth of that old Indian legend that you cannot scalp a bald man. However, that trouble has been satisfactorily overcome. I am hopeful that with a return to normal production and prosperity generally, we shall see millions of bushels of grain going through Churchill. I hope to see not only grain but other farm products, as well as a considerable incoming, movement of domestic requirements. After all, no port can hope for ultimate success without both incoming and outgoing freight haulage.

The hon. member for
Melville (Mr. Motherwell) has always been a great booster for the Hudson Bay railway; but I regret that on certain occasions when he could have exerted more influence to have this route built a little earlier, he did not take advantage of his opportunities. I can remember when the hon. member was interested in an election in 1908. We have a splendid theatre building in my town, and I can still remember the motto that was displayed at a Liberal meeting. It read: "Laurier will build the Hudson Bay railway, not to-morrow but now." We know when it was built; it was years later. The hon. member has always been a booster for this route, and I was glad to hear him express himself as he did.

There was one remark made by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) to which I should like to take exception. He said that he hoped he would live long enough to see Montreal made a winter port. I am sure we all wish the hon. member for Melville, who is one of the grand old men of this house, many years of life, but I certainly do not wish to see him live long enough to see the port of Montreal one of the winter ports of Canada.
Why not?

"Why not?" The maritime
provinces have made sacrifices continually for the rest of Canada. Why should the western provinces, in order to save a few cents in freight rates on grain, which I assume would be the reason, wise to sacrifice the ports of Saint John and Halifax? That sort of thing has been going on for years; it is a sentiment which we in the maritime provinces resent very much, and I believe that sentiment is not shared iby many in western Canada and in other parts of this country.
The minister stated that the expenditures at the port of Churchill might be found under another item. Is it under national harbours?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay railway-construction and improvements-capital, $25,000.
What is the nature of this expenditure?

This is just a capital vote.
The amount asked for is required to continue the work started in 1908 on the Hudson Bay railway project. The construction of the railway is practically completed, and the

road is in good operating condition although it is likely for several years to require a certain amount of ballasting and drain filling to make up for the settlement and shrinkage which will undoubtedly occur in the embankments. This amount will provide for the excavation of off-take ditches, the elimination of timber trestles and the construction of cedar culverts where additional openings are required.

Item agreed to.
Maritime Freight Rates Act-
To hereby authorize and provide for the payment from time to time during the fiscal year 1938-39 to the Canadian National Railway Company of the difference (estimated by the auditors of the said company and certified by the said auditors to the Minister of Transport as and when required by the said minister) occurring on account of the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, between the tariff tolls and the normal tolls (upon the same basis as set out in section 9 of the said act with respect to companies therein referred to) on all traffic moved during the year 1938, under the tariffs approved, on the eastern lines (as referred to in section 1 of the said act) of the Canadian National Railways, $2,278,000.

This item was considered
and approved in the railway committee, but I assume it should be called here.

How is the increase of
8478,000	made up?

As was explained in the
railway committee, this is a statutory item and the increased requirement is due to increased business.

The minister anticipates
that?

Yes. It is twenty per cent of whatever business moves under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. We had to supply a deficit on last year's operations, which has appeared in the supplementaries for last year. This year we are appropriating approximately the actual cost of last year.

Coal & Kailway Company; New Brunswick Coal & Railway Company, Cumberland Railway & Coal Company, Dominion Atlantic Railway, Maritime Coal, Railway & Power Company, Sydney & Louisburg Railway, Temiscouata Railway Company, $860,000.

Yes. The previous item applied to the Canadian National Railways, and this one applies to the Canadian Pacific railway and other railways which receive payments under that act.
To railways other than the Canadian National.

Interest on rails rolled for Canadian National Railways: To provide for payment of interest under the terms and conditions of orders in council P.C. 1462 and P.C. 1533 of June 7, 1935, respecting orders of steel rails for the Canadian National Railway Company, $30,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

Under the Public Works Construction Act of 1935. orders were placed for steel rails in anticipation of requirements, the provision being that the government advance to the railways a portion of the cost of the rails and undertake to pay interest on the balance until the rails were required. These rails have been gradually taken into stock as the railways could use them, and the $30,000 represents the interest on the rails which are still in store at the steel plants, and of which the railways have not taken delivery.
Has the minister any idea when delivery is likely to be taken and the complete obligation terminated?

We are taking this year all our rails except a certain amount of 130-pound rails. The main line improvements have not been proceeding rapidly enough to give us any assurance when we shall be able to take the last of the 130-pound rails, but I think it will be in two or three years.

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bertrand (Laurier) for the second reading of Bill No. 28, to amend the criminal code.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BT PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
It is almost two months since we started discussing this question. When the debate was adjourned on the last occasion I intended to quote Mr. Peter McGibbon, at one time member of parliament for Muskoka, Ontario. In 1934 Mr. McGibbon said:
I am more concerned with the possibilities for good, with the amelioration of the sufferings of humanity, and the lessening of the economic wastage of the human machine through the instrumentality of this bill than I am with the methods or the disputed morality connected with it.
The abjections to this bill are all directed from the point of view of morality. I have received a large number of letters from persons throughout the country, a few in protest and also some marked copies of newspapers, to which I should like to direct the attention of the house. I have here a copy of The New Outlook, which, I believe, is published in Toronto. It is a marked copy, and there is in it an article entitled " Sweepstakes; a Moral Issue." The moral issue seems to be the scarecrow argument against sweepstakes. Here is an article that is typical . of a large number of others written against the bill. The author is a Mr. Mutchmor, who gives as his qualification the fact that he is associate secretary, department of social service and evangelism. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to bear that in mind- evangelism. I want to show how charitable the evangelists are in this instance. This is what the writer says:
"With an Ontario-Quebec gang-up" to compel the federal government to amend section 236 of the criminal code in order that Mr. Bertrand's bill to legalize sweepstakes may be passed, we find ourselves in danger of a gambling craze similar to that experienced just after the war. Mr. Bertrand stated in the House of Commons that such legalized sweepstakes would help the Catholic university of Montreal. Such an argument is hardly sufficient, when we consider the moral issues at stake.
I have already quoted another author who wrote on lotteries, H. M. Muller. She has
2S61
Criminal Code[DOT]-Sweepstakes

given a good deal of information and considerable data in relation to sweepstakes and lotteries. At page 64 I find the following:
The records show that by an act of parliament money was raised by lottery for the British Museum. Also England provided money for our Virginia colonists by means of a lottery. Thomas Jefferson heartily endorsed a lottery created by congress. John Adams and Benjamin Franklin obtained a "lottery loan" to meet government bills.
And so on.
I wish to call the attention of the house to one extremely uncharitable paragraph in Mr. Mutchmor's article. He says:
Perhaps one of the greatest moral weaknesses, if the proposed bill is passed, will reveal itself in the civil service.
All we are asking the house to do is to pass a bill which will permit of the organization of lotteries under the absolute control of the legislatures, and this gentleman who is typical of all those who are opposed to the bill, declares that the weakness is in the civil service. He says:
Corrupt practices endanger good government. We knew that before he said it.
We raise some pertinent questions: Who will receive the printing contracts? Which political friends will have the commission and sale of tickets? Whose nephews and nieces, cousins and sweethearts-
Mark you, Mr. Speaker, "sweethearts."
-will be employed as stenographers and clerks? The state has too small a credit on its moral ledger to extend any more business privileges to such a group as the gambling fraternity.
I strongly protest against such articles. Merely because we wish to give the provinces the right to permit the organization of lotteries for charitable purposes, I do not see how we can be opposed on the ground that the object is to give employment to cousins or nephews or sweethearts or anybody else.

Well, perhaps a lot of people who did not vote are of my opinion. Anyhow those who took the trouble to vote were three to one in favour of lotteries.
Since this bill was introduced, something very important happened. There was a drawing for the Irish Sweepstakes for the benefit of the hospitals in Ireland. The newspapers tell us that in Toronto alone there were about
300,000	people who had bought tickets, and that three times a year Torontonians were buying tickets to the extent of $1,000,000 each time. Does it not strike anyone that this money which is going to foreign countries should be made to stay here?

enacted, would it stop the sale of Irish Sweepstakes tickets in this country?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BT PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext: My answer is that it would stop it to the extent that legislation for the control of liquor has stopped the illicit sale of liquor. I do not see why, if the government of Ontario or Quebec or any other province are interested in selling something for the benefit of their hospitals or universities, they would not go to the trouble of stopping illicit sale. I am sure they would to a very large extent. I do not know why any Canadian would buy tickets for the Irish Sweepstakes when he, could buy a ticket here the benefit of which would go to a charitable institution in Canada.

speechtext: Well, that is a question. I would not go to the extent of agreeing with my hon. friend, who implies by his question that the 300,000 Torontonians who buy tickets are buying them just for the sake of winning a large amount of money. It is the pleasure of buying the tickets.

speechtext:
The average
intelligence of Canadians is high enough to know the chances they have when they buy a ticket. But they buy it for the pleasure of
it. And the pleasure would be much greater if they knew that the money was going to be invested in something that would benefit the community. We have a law which was passed in 1936. I do not know whether hon. members realize that when the best newspapers of Canada published last March the results of the drawing of the Irish Sweepstakes they were committing a criminal offence for which the president or general manager could be sent to gaol for one year. I have some newspapers here, among them Le Canada, which is a good newspaper, the Montreal Gazette, the Toronto Globe and Mail, all the newspapers of Ottawa; yet according to this law passed in 1936 amending the criminal code they committed an offence for which the manager or president could be sent to gaol for one year. It shows the fallacy of such laws. Let me read it. I leave out the words which are not necessary for the purpose of this argument. It is 1 Edward VIII, chapter 29, paragraph 7, amending section 227 of the criminal code. Common betting place is now defined as:
.	.	. an office, room or place which is
opened, kept or used for the purpose of facilitating or encouraging or assisting in the making of bets upon horse races by announcing the results of horse races whether such horse race takes place in Canada or elsewhere.
If we have reached the stage where we can put upon our statutes laws creating criminal offences which can be committed publicly right at the door of parliament, it is about time that we see to it, when we know that so many millions are going out of the country for this purpose.
I said the purpose of the bill is not to encourage the gambling habit; it is to keep that money here-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BT PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS

Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member introduced his bill on March 15, he gave us his arguments in support of this measure, and I think that this evening he has added very little to those arguments.
First of all, he claims that this measure will put an end to illegality. That is a mere statement; there has been no information brought forward indicating that it will work in that way, and although one cannot bring statistical proof in a matter of this kind, undoubtedly general experience would seem to indicate that legalizing sweepstakes rather tends to encourage the practice of gambling. In any case there has been no evidence whatever brought before this house that it would put an end to it.
Again we are told that legislation of this kind might divert some of the money which now goes to Ireland. Again that is a hope, but notwithstanding what the hon. member has said to-night-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BT PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
