subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BT PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
That is entirely another matter. This is not going to stop it; there is no evidence whatever that it will do so. In my judgment, which I give for what it is worth, if we go in for this sort of thing and encourage it, it is more likely to lead to still larger amounts going to Ireland or any other place where people think they can get something for nothing.
We are being asked to endorse this measure on the ground that it will help to support hospitals and universities, particularly the university of Montreal. Well, I am not going to be led away by an appeal for sympathy for one particular institution in one particular province. In dealing with the criminal code we should think of the whole of Canada, the welfare of all the people, rather than the welfare of some particular institution. I go down to Montreal now and I find that they support their hospitals, in part at least, by a tax on food. You cannot get a meal in a restaurant without paying that tax. I do not see why the wealthy municipality of Montreal and the comparatively wealthy province of Quebec cannot support these hospitals, as other provinces are able to do, through the taxes of the people or through voluntary effort.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BT PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext: This is a tax.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BT PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS
speechtext:
No, no. I wonder
that the hon. member suggests that; I cannot see anything analogous to a tax in this proposal. The hon. member says:
-if this bill were passed almost everybody, even the unemployed, would readily buy a ticket to take a chance on a sweepstake for the benefit of our hospitals and universities.
The hon. gentleman has just said that this is a tax; and, if it is a tax, he proposes to tax even the unemployed. That is going a long way. I should say the equitable way- decent thing-would be to tax the wealthy, who can easily afford to pay such a tax, not to try to wring it out of the poor people, even the unemployed, on the odd chance of their winning something. What a policy! Extract the very last drop from the poor, in the vain hope that by taking a chance of this kind they may get something out of it!
The hon. member administered a rebuke to the Social Service Council of Canada., Possibly it was merited; that is, if we interpret that statement which was read into Hansard as meaning we should not pass this legislation because of the effect it might have on church givings. I am not quite sure whether or not that is what it means, but I would say that churches and charitable institutions are in a veiy bad way indeed if they must live through the avails of a prostituted desire for gain. I hope the churches and charitable institutions have not sunk quite so low as that.
The hon. gentleman goes back several hundred years and tells us that some of the big universities were founded through lotteries. I have not checked that statement; it may be so, but in those days we had slavery and a great many other evils which we have since outgrown. He says the universities were bora in sin but they are not looked down upon to-day. Well, to put it in other words, that means that the end justifies the means. I think that is one of the ideas underlying the appeal we have heard tonight, that the end justifies the means. Some of us cannot accept that teaching.

I do not know whether or not he will laud that, but to be consistent he should be rather inclined to look to Vancouver for a lead along this line.

It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this country was founded on the ideal that prosperity should come to people not through chance but rather as the reward of patient industry. I do not think it is in the interest of our people that we khould turn ourselves into a nation of gamblers even to support the various concerns that need assistance. We have generally gone on the principle that people should support worthy institutions either by means of taxation or by means of voluntary contributions. Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate because of convictions which may be just as strong as those which prompted the hon. member to sponsor the measure. May I, first of all, congratulate him upon the literature he has been reading lately. We have been taught by our early teachers that the more we read about a thing the more we become like it; I would say that the New Outlook would come in the first rank of clean literature in Canada, and I should like at this time to pay tribute to Mr. Mutchmor, the social worker who wrote the article. I know the gentleman well; he is a better man than I am. I might not compare favourably with the hon. member who sponsored the measure, but I do know that Mr. Mutchmor is a better man than I am, morally, spiritually and intellectually. It is for that reason I believe that he would compare favourably with the best men in the house.
I did not get my reasons for opposing the bill from the New Outlook; I got them from my dad when I was a very small boy, at a time when I bet threepence on a donkey race. My dad talked to me reasonably and sensibly, and I believe that at that time the desire for gambling was nipped in the bud. I did not see much good in it then, and I do not see any good in it now.
I have three reasons for opposing the bill, and in the first place I would put the economic reason. A system of sweepstakes would be bad economics. I am sure there is not a member in the house who would not do his best to find some economic system which would kill unemployment, which would bring production to the highest point and distribution to the point of perfection, and all with the least possibly injury to any human being. I am convinced, however, that this end cannot be achieved by instituting a system of sweepstakes. When we are laying the foundations for the youth of Canada, the land of our adoption, we must think of those people in church, state and business who have tried to keep God first and others next. I am convinced that they have laid the foundation well, and woe betide the individuals who would try to switch us from that rock, the foundation on which we build.
The hon. member has said we should keep our money in Canada. I am wondering if there would be any sweepstakes tickets sold
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

in the United States. As a boy I was taught that if I gave anything for a benevolent purpose, whether it was for a hospital or for a charity of some kind. I was to forget about it. When a man spends $2.50 he should expect to get at least three per cent for his money. I believe the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) would say that that is a reasonable amount.

That may be so in theory, but it is not true in practice. If I buy a sweepstakes ticket, I am throwing in my lot with all the rest in the hope of getting $150,000, or some other enormous sum.
It has been said that licence kills or hurts the drink business. I am not so sure about that, and especially when I see that in Ontario we have a drink bill amounting to $72,000,000, a sum of money which would put a great many people to work. Who buy the sweepstakes tickets? We do not find any of the Scotch buying them-at least not many of the Scotch. They do not buy because they recognize that a system of sweepstakes is bad economics and represents a poor investment. We do not find any of our Hebrew brethren buying sweepstakes tickets; they recognize them as a bad investment and very poor economics. For the government to invite people to speculate, without even the pretence of promoting industry, is to hinder recovery, check stabilization and frustrate orderly development.
I find that the intelligent press is against sweepstakes, and in that connection I would quote the Ottawa Journal. Had I the time I could quote the Montreal Herald and the Montreal Gazette along similar lines. The Ottawa Journal makes the statement that lotteries are bad and, without reading the editorial may I point out that not one sentence

in it is in favour of a system of sweepstakes. I was amused when at one point the editor states:
The comparison of sweepstake with a horse race or a modest bingo game is far from exact. In the one case there is the element of amusement and the wager, if an important by-product, still is not the whole thing. But money spent for a sweepstake ticket brings no such return in entertainment.
A group of Chinamen may sit around a table and play their game of hong kong-or whatever you call it-and have a little fun. But when one buys a sweepstakes ticket I wonder what fun he gets from it?
The argument I use with greatest force and sincerity is that it is bad morality. The old commandment says: "Thou shalt not covet." I read somewhere that if you break the moral law, the moral law will break you. We must remember the commandment: "Thou shalt not covet." I do not think the parliament of Canada, with its three great divisions of King, Senate and House of Commons, can improve upon that moral law.
When I buy a sweepstakes ticket for $2.50, what do I expect to receive in return? I expect a return not only from my ticket but from the tickets of thousands of others, possibly 400,000 of them. It is bad morality, and it is a system whereby we covet what the other man has or may expect to get. When we attempt to support hospitals by sweepstakes and an appeal to the gambling spirit we are using a low method of supporting; any cause, whether it be moral or philanthropic.
Mr. Speaker, I say most respectfully that 1 try to reach the chamber on time each day regularly so that I may hear you coming before a great parliament and praying to lead us not into temptation. Yet I see people going through the country trying to convince our youth to buy sweepstakes tickets. I see a man of mature years approaching a young man and saying to him, "Here is a sweepstakes ticket; it will cost you only $2.50; take a chance." What is that man doing? It is against the temptations of such men that iwe must pray, "Lead us not into temptation." Those men are leading the youth into temptation when they offer tickets for sale at $2.50.
I cannot but think of some of the great institutions in Canada that get along very well without subscriptions of this type. We must take off our hats and pay our respects to an organization like the Salvation Army which does its work without respect of persons. If they resorted to sweepstakes for funds to carry on their work, they would be

Criminal Code-Sweepstakes
doomed. They have far more sense than to do that. The Canadian people do not need to have their sense of generosity stimulated by the hope of winning a sweepstake.
It is bad polities. I have great admiration for the premier of Ontario because I believe he has done many great things. However, I disagree with him in his stand on this question. I admire the members of his government who would not support the principle of sweepstakes. If I supported this resolution, I would be giving the premier of Ontario the right to give me a special appellation.
It is bad morality and it is bad politics. In 1906 an act was passed in England prohibiting betting and wagering in the public streets. That country understood the viciousness of anything in the way of sweepstakes. I should like to quote an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of May 3, reading as follows:
Contrary to universal opinion, the hospitals of Ireland are not in clover because of returns from sweepstakes, to which money is contributed from all quarters of the globe.
The Montreal Gazette is opposed to the principle of sweepstakes because it is bad morality, bad economics and bad politics. An editorial in the Montreal Herald reads as follows:
Medical men of Dublin, Ireland, are attacking the hospital sweepstakes, declaring that they have greatly injured the voluntary hospitals of the city.
At the annual charter dinner of the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, prominent medical men and others attacked the system.
They declared that the sweepstakes were started to help the hospitals but the government had stepped in and was collecting a tax of twenty-five per cent of the funds and diverting it to other causes. Out of this had sprung a demand for a municipal hospital and the scrapping of some of the voluntary hospitals which have been useful for many years. The protests may develop into a concerted drive against the sweepstakes.
Both the Montreal Gazette and the Montreal Herald are opposed to the introduction of sweepstakes into Canada. Many of our leading citizens are also opposed to sweepstakes. We have only to look around us here in this chamber to see many who are opposed to sweepstakes. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has declared himself against this thing. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has declared himself against sweepstakes. The Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) took action in the city of Brandon and would not permit advertising of sweepstakes to be carried through the mails. I take off my hat to the Postmaster General for taking that action. I pray that 51952-182
it will not be long before he is back in the house. I admire him for his courage and the willingness to do the square thing. I see another man in this house who is opposed to sweepstakes, a gentleman whom I have known for forty years, the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth). I would imagine that the leader of the social credit group (Mr. Blackmore) is also against sweepstakes because he does not believe in handing out money without getting something in return. Another reason for his opposition would be his own personal Christian character and his good, sound economic common sense.
It is the task of every good citizen to oppose gambling in every form, whether it is said to be for a good or for a selfish purpose. Our leaders have given us the lead and it is our duty to follow. I agree with those who say that we have no right to tell a man how he should spend his money. But, when it becomes a matter of public policy, we should let our judgment and conscience speak. The foundation of our great country is laid upon our faith in God and the common welfare of, our fellow men, and we should not be afraid to take a stand and vote against something which is not in the best interests of our fellow citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for a few minutes before the house adjourned just six weeks ago-when the defence estimates were last up for consideration-I had been dealing with the problem of the defence of Canada's Pacific coast. I had pointed out that for the protection of that coast against major attacks this government seemed to be relying upon the American navy, there being no British navy within seven thousand miles, the nearest naval unit being at Singapore. I had also pointed out that there was no adequate defence on the Pacific coast a.t the present time against minor attacks, such as hit-and-run raids by ships carrying aircraft, and attacks to establish bases on our coast. I think the Minister of National Defence will admit that so far we have not on the Pacific coast adequate defences to protect ourselves against these minor attacks. I think he will also admit that defence against minor attacks is what is known throughout the British commonwealth as local defence, and as such is the responsibility of Canada alone. That principle has been established throughout the commonwealth for many years, and I would refer the members of the committee particularly to the summary of the proceedings of the imperial conference held in 1923, at page 16, in paragraph 3 (a):
Subject to this provision, the conference suggests the following as guiding principles:
(a) The primary responsibility of each portion of the empire represented at the conference for its own local defence.
That principle was reaffirmed at the imperial conference in 1926, and again at the conference in 1937. At all three conferences the Canadian delegation was headed by our present Prime Minister. The principle means simply that Canada must defend her own coasts 51952-182}
against minor attacks; and as minor attacks are the only danger at the present time, on the Pacific coast at least it means that those Canadians who live on the Pacific slope must look to the Canadian defence forces for protection.
There is the problem; and while the government is doing something about it-and I give the government and the Minister of National Defence credit for what has been done in the way of improving our defences on the Pacific coast-I submit that this government is failing utterly to deal with some aspects of the problem. I believe its greatest failure is that it has not provided, and apparently is not taking steps to provide, for an adequate coastal defence fleet. It is obvious that we must have such a fleet. The minister himself so stated during the Easter recess, and if the newspaper report from which I propose to quote is not accurate, I would ask him to correct it. It is an article appearing in the Vancouver Daily Province reporting the minister's speech in that city two or three weeks ago, and reads in part:
For defence of our focal sea areas we need sea and air forces capable of destroying hostile surface craft, submarines and air raiders. This requires reconnaissance, fighter and torpedocarrying aircraft, and adequate naval strength
Then he went on to say:
To defend our neutrality wre need constant patrol of our coastal area by auxiliary surface craft and aircraft, bombing aircraft to destroy bases, means to dispatch small expeditions.
It is contemplated that naval and aircraft will patrol the entire eoast from their respective stations.
That all means that we must have an adequate fleet on the Pacific coast. He might also have mentioned the fact that we have on that coast to-day at least 1.200 Japanese fishing vessels operating in and out of the different harbours and ports, which might have to be dealt with in the event of hostilities with Japan. In his speech in introducing the defence estimates, the minister said as reported at page 1647 of Hansard:
A certain amount of priority has been established after deliberation: first for the air services; secondly, for naval defence; and thirdly, in regard to the repairing of deficiencies in equipment of militia services, permanent and non-permanent.
That is the position taken by the government itself; yet what do we find? In these estimates provision is made only for two secondhand or used destroyers, which are to be purchased from Great Britain. These ships are to be placed on the Pacific coast where we shall then have four destroyers and two mine-sweepers. That will be the extent of our fleet. Apparently the government is
Supply-National Defence

buying odd ships from year to year; it appears to have no plan whatever as to the size of a Canadian navy or as to the time when it is to be completed.
If there is a plan, it should be announced. The Canadian people should be taken into the confidence of the government just as has been done in Great Britain and Australia; within the past few weeks we have seen press reports of the ships to be added to those other empire fleets; surely the Canadian people are entitled to have similar information with regard to the Canadian navy. One would think that the Department of National Defence would at least have decided upon the minimum naval requirements for the local defence of the Canadian coasts. If so, the Canadian people should know what that plan is. If the department has not such a plan, it is derelict in its duty.
I can find no report anywhere of plans for a Canadian navy. The only thing of the kind I have been able to trace is the recommendation submitted by Admiral Jellicoe when he came to Canada in 1919 on a naval mission at the request of the then Canadian government; he recommended in his report, at page 10, chapter 1, dealing with the naval requirements of Canada, paragraph 4:
The question of the naval forces required by Canada may be viewed in two ways: first, in the light of Canada's own requirements, and Canada's own safety; and secondly, in the broader light of the security and safety of the empire as a whole. The naval force suggested as adequate purely for the protection of Canada's trade and Canada's ports under tne conditions assumed, comprises-
And this is what he recommends as a minimum for a Canadian defence navy:
-three light cruisers, one flotilla leader-
Which, I believe, is a large destroyer.
-twelve torpedo craft, eight submarines, with one parent ship, and certain auxiliary small craft for training purposes, etc.
That was immediately after the great war when the danger was nothing like what it is at the present time. It does seem perfectly clear that in Canada we require at least one or two flotilla leaders and more destroyers as well as submarines, motor torpedo boats, and submarine chasers which can be used to attack hostile fleets. We have at the present time no ships for that purpose. We also require craft for laying out and protecting mine fields and a mosquito fleet to patrol and protect our inlets. All these small craft could operate only within a few miles of our coasts, so that no one could say they were for purposes of aggression. I suggest that a coastal defence fleet of this type might be

established this year-not in four or five years, but this year-by borrowing ships held by Great Britain in reserve. I understand that they have many ships of this type being held in their ports in reserve, which could be on loan until Canada had completed her own navy. Many of the smaller ships could be built here. We have shipyards that could do that work, and it would give a great stimulus to the shipbuilding industry of the country. The government could take steps at once to start a building program for the construction of a defence fleet. So much for the navy.
Then, I submit that the government is not facing the problem of defending our coasts, because it is taking no adequate steps to have not only ships but also aircraft, guns, munitions and equipment manufactured in Canada. There is a plaintive wailing by the government about being unable to buy: they cannot buy anything; their hands are tied. The minister said, as reported at page 1648 of Hansard:
Difficulty has been experienced with reference to obtaining deliveries, and that has accounted for another part of the reduction.
At page 1649:
With reference to militia services there has been carried out by the department what is known as an interim plan of armaments for both coasts. This is a result of the fact that heavy ordnance cannot be acquired from British concerns for a period of about three years.
In other words, we have to sit back and be inadequately defended for a period of three years. Canada might just as well face the fact now that other nations are too busy preparing to defend themselves to be able to sell us arms; that if Great Britain is at war we cannot expect to get war material from her; and that future wars will be largely mechanized, requiring primarily machines which we are able to manufacture in this country if only we have the energy to do so.
Then, the government is not facing the problem of defending the Pacific coast, because it is not setting up naval or defence reserves on that coast. There are many strategic points on the mainland and the islands which should be held by the government; the property there should be acquired. There is nothing at all now to prevent, for example, the Japanese government from indirectly acquiring land, timber rights or mineral rights, at these strategic points or near our bases or fortifications. As a matter of fact, we hear rumour after rumour that such is the case. This is not good enough; the government should reserve these strategic points. I suggest to the minister, with all the seriousness I can, that, he have a survey

Supply-National Defence
made as soon as possible of the ownership of the land and timber and mineral rights at these strategic points and near fortifications and bases, and particularly a survey such that it will show which of these lands and rights are held by or for foreigners.
The government is also failing to face the necessity, from a military point of view, of highways to the Pacific coast. At present we have no highway across British Columbia. The trans-Canada highway is impassable because there is a gap of about thirty-three miles; the government builds a little this year, a little next year; it is to be completed in 1939, we hope; but that road should be completed at once, because it is a strategic road. Further, there is no road through southern British Columbia; there is a gap in the Princeton-Hope road of about thirty-seven miles, which should also be built for strategic purposes; and we should have a highway through to Prince Rupert or Stewart. These would all be strategic highways and should be the concern of the Department of National Defence as well as, say the Department of Mines and Resources.
Finally, in connection with the failure of the government to face this problem of defending the Pacific coast, I doubt very much whether there are sufficient trained men in British Columbia to man the fortifications we have there, or will have, to protect the bases, and to repel raiders. I believe there are one or two hundred men of the permanent force-the minister can correct me if I am wrong-and according to the last report of the department, about 2,550 men of the militia. That is the total number who underwent training. I suggest that the minister allow the British Columbia units to recruit up to a strength which will provide the people in that province with a force sufficient to man the fortifications, protect the bases and repel raids; further that these militiamen on the coast should be fully equipped at once and given the best training possible. It is not fair to men who volunteer to risk their lives in the defence of the country to leave them half-equipped and half-trained. Nothing is more unfair on the part of a national government.
I suggest that these features of the problem of defence of our coasts are sufficiently serious to warrant an investigation this year by a special committee of this house, representative of all parties. I believe it would be possible for us to agree unanimously on a policy for the local defence of our coasts. That agreement can best be obtained if the government will set up a special committee, with all parties represented on it, and place
all the facts before that committee. So much for the problem of local defence.
Turning to the broader aspects of Canada's defence problem, the minister admitted, and I think will admit to-night, that Canadians can defend themselves against major attacks only by cooperating with other nations; for example, on the Atlantic with the British fleet. It is quite clear that Canada must cooperate with the other nations of the British commonwealth. Actually the government is doing so now, but will not admit it. This pretence that we are not cooperating with the other nations of the British commonwealth, this "Hush, hush" policy, misleads the Canadian people and weakens the British Commonwealth of Nations in the eyes of the other nations of the world, and the result is to hurt us here as far as the defence of our country is concerned. Actually every Canadian government since the war has cooperated in defence measures with the other nations of the commonwealth. One has only to refer to the imperial conference summaries for 1923, 1926, 1937. Our present Prime Minister was in command of the Canadian delegation at each of those conferences, and we find the principle laid down as clearly as possible that Canada is to cooperate with the other nations of the empire in defence. In 1923 they stressed naval bases at page 16 of the summary of proceedings: in 1926, air bases, at page 29. Then I quote from the summary of proceedings for 1937 at page 12:
Though -we shall discuss other important sublets- we are agreed that questions of foreign affairs and defence shall be our main subjects.
At page 1649:
The conference gave close attention to the subject of defence, and considered ways in which it would be possible for the governments concerned to cooperate in measures for their own security. The occasion was taken for a detailed review- of the state of defence in each of the countries represented at the conference and this opportunity was generally welcomed.
At page 18:
The conference recognized the vital importance of measures to safeguard maritime communications, including routes and waterways essential to defence and trade, and to provide naval bases and facilities for repairs and fuelling of ships.
At page 19:
The conference also recorded the progress made by the several governments in creating and maintaining an adequate chain of air bases and refuelling stations along the lines of communications between the different parts of the empire.
The conference noted with satisfaction that in accordance with recommendations of previous conferences a common system of organization and training and the use of uniform
Supply-National Defence

manuals, patterns of arms, equipment, and stores had been adopted, as far as practicable, for the naval, military and air forces of their several countries. Each of them would thus be enabled to ensure more effectively its own security and, if it so desired, to cooperate with other countries of the Commonwealth with the least possible delay. The interchange of individual officers of the naval, military and air forces of the countries was recognized as conducing to the dissemination of the experience acquired by the officers concerned under the widely different conditions existing in various parts of the empire .	.	.
The conference gave careful attention to the question of munitions and supplies required for defence both by the United Kingdom and other parts of the Commonwealth, and also to the question of the supply of food and feeding stuffs in time of emergency.
In other words, Canada is in alliance for defensive purposes with our kinfolk, the other nations of the British commonwealth. It is the safest and wisest defence program we could adopt. All these British nations are aiming at peace and not war. At page 13 of last year's imperial conference summary we find this:
Thus they agreed that for each member of the commonwealth the first objective is the preservation of peace. In their view the settlement of differences that may arise between nations and the adjustment of national needs should be sought by methods of cooperation, joint inquiry and conciliation. It is in such methods, and not in recourse to the use of force between nation and nation, that the surest guarantee will be found for the improvement of international relations and respect for mutual engagements.
Holding these views and desiring to base their policies upon the aims and ideals of the league of nations, they found themselves unanimous in declaring that their respective armaments will never be used for purposes of aggression or for any purpose inconsistent with the covenant of the league of nations or the pact of Paris.
Then, further down on page 14:
Being convinced that the influence of each of them in the cause of peace was likely to be greatly enhanced by their common agreement to use that influence in the same direction, they declared their intention of continuing to consult and cooperate with one another in this vital interest and all matters of common concern.
It is our safest course because all the nations of the commonwealth are trying to agree on the fundamental principles of foreign policy. For example, they are all trying to collaborate with the United States of America. Further, we know these peoples of the British nations; we know we can depend upon them; we know we can trust them. Those of us who served overseas know that, if trouble arises, you can have no better men beside you than the men from the other parts of the British Empire. There is very little risk of one nation of the commonwealth doing anything that will drag the others into war. We have seen that

within the last few weeks, in the attitude taken by the Prime Minister of Great Britain. And remember this. Mr. Chairman: Any Canadian foreign policy necessarily must involve some risk, and my submission is that any other policy than that of working with the other nations of the empire would involve far more serious risks.
My complaint against this government is that instead of focusing the attention of the Canadian people on the fact that our foreign policy actually is a defensive alliance with the other nations of the commonwealth, with peace as the aim, and collaboration with the United States and friendliness with all nations, this government keeps harping on the fact that its hands are free, that it has no commitments. This government says: "Oh, we can be informed by the British government of what goes on; but we cannot be consulted, because that might involve some obligation upon us." as though the policy of working with the other nations of the British commonwealth were something to be ashamed of. This attitude on the part of the government is entirely out of line with the courage and clear-sightedness of the Canadian people. In my opinion the government policy could be best described as spineless.
F'inally, in considering the question of Canadian defence and Canadian foreign policy one instinctively thinks of the nationhood of the Canadian people and of the Canada of the future. As a nation we have done many worthwhile things. For example, our part in the great war gained us the respect of all the civilized countries of the world. The part we have played in the League of Nations has been more outstanding than that of any other nation in the Americas. Like Great Britain, we have done what we could to further disarmament among the nations. We have become one of the leading nations of that group which ranks immediately after the seven great world powers; in fact, I believe even in population Canada is among the first twenty nations of the world. Canada is now at a fork in the road1. Are we going to bury our heads in the sand, -and depend upon other peoples for our defence, which means for our very existence? Are we going to refuse to look beyond the borders of Canada? I would suggest that the attitude of this government would lead any reasonable Canadian to believe that such was the case at the present time. If we take that road, probably we shall end up as a small American republic. Or are we going to continue to be a nation, taking a worthwhile part in world1 affairs, facing these problems

Supply-National Defence
of defence and foreign policy frankly and fearlessly and letting the other nations of the world know exactly where we stand, yet with world peace always our main objective? This government, with its great majority, the largest number of followers any Canadian government has ever had-I sometimes think they would be glad to lose a few of them-should be the strongest government Canada has ever had. It has a great opportunity to give leadership to the Canadian people in connection with these problems. If it will remember the Canadian character; if it will act with the initiative, the soundness, the friendliness and the courage of the Canadian people, it will not delay any longer in leading them along the second road.

speechtext:
That is a different proposition. I do not think the people of Japan are any more desirous of having their young men go out and be killed than we are. I do not think China is any more desirous of war than any other nation. I do not think Italy desires war. The fact that the government of a country has thrown that country into war does not mean that the people share that desire. That is one thing that we are contending right in this country. If we went to war, would it be a case of the people desiring that war? I shall speak of that a little later on in my address; but I believe we have taken the wrong road, and I
believe we are still taking the wrong road if we are looking for a permanent solution of this question of war.
From speeches I have heard in this house; as I have read the press, and from articles that have appeared on different occasions I have come to the conclusion that the greatest strife in this world is competition, which travels through nations, through dominions, through municipalities and right down to the individual. We have always contended that competition was the life of world trade; but I am not so sure that this has been the correct reasoning, especially when we look about us and see that, almost without exception, in the end this rivalry in trade leads to war. I think we had a very good example of that not so long ago in connection with the oil industry of Mexico, which showed just how nations may become involved in competition for trade and through large financial concerns. Rightly or wrongly the Mexican government took possession of the oil fields of that country. Immediately we had representations made by the governments of the United States and Great Britain in an endeavour to get back those oil fields. In that case I think it was the financial interests who were influencing the government, more than it was the desires of the people. Surely that was Mexico's own business. Yet we were interfering there with another nation in connection with the control of its natural resources. Whether that control was or was not going to be carried out to the best advantage of all concerned, we cannot say. Yet that was their policy.
I believe if we go back to find out the causes of war we would be getting nearer the solution. I am thinking now of war in the broader sense, and not of the war where there are battles for the purpose of killing people. We have war in the state from the rivalry of individuals. Man has to make a living; so he is continually combating his neighbour for a better economical situation, and this combat leads to keen rivalry. The individual reaches the state where he becomes financially embarrassed and must appeal to the municipality. The municipality on the other hand becomes equally financially distressed, and looks around for help. The municipalities must do that because they find great competition in financial matters. It is their desire to get a greater amount of revenue. Finding themselves at a loss they turn to provincial authorities, which are already overtaxed. It is not possible for the provinces to increase their revenues and so, in turn, they come to the only source left,
Supply-National Defence

namely the dominion. Then, the dominion is so overwhelmingly in debt that it has almost reached the limit of its possibility of getting greater revenue. Facing that condition, the dominion must endeavour to borrow from other nations. It must try to meet its debts by increased trade, and eventually conditions become so intense that a physical war breaks out.
I read the other day an interesting quotation from the observations of Henry W. Morgan of Montreal, chairman of the executive of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, in which he stated that to-day Canada had piled up an indebtedness of over eight billions of dollars, or about S800 per person. He pointed out, and properly so, that this huge debt would go on piling up indefinitely, and that inevitably there must come a day of reckoning.
We now have a rearmament program in which we are about to spend 834,000,000. In Great Britain they are spending thirty-eight billions of dollars or about 8800 per person. There is a new seven and a half billion rearmament plan, and it will continue to grow. In the United States the national debt is about thirty-nine billions, or $325 per person; they have a new five and a half billion dollar rearmament plan, and it is still growing.
Where will this economic system lead us? Does anyone think that these huge debts can be paid out of taxation, or in some way, by people or governments, or that any government will solve this problem of debt by simply creating another debt? Our present debt system requires the formation of a system of national credit for the creation of wealth and happiness for our citizens.
We are coming closer to the real cause of war when our financing puts us into such a position that it is almost impossible for us to go ahead and prepare for war without creating a still greater national debt, a national debt which we shall never in the world pay off. The other day I was speaking with respect to debt to a very able man in this city, and he said he did not believe that it would ever be paid off, and added he believed that theoretically it would be wrong to pay it off. Yet we are going ahead and taxing our people. Over fifty per cent of the taxes they pay goes to pay interest on our tremendous debt. Without exception, every country in the world faces a similar situation.
What is the cause of this debt? Why has it reached such dimensions? I believe one of the greatest trading opportunities we have is right around us; our greatest market is right here in Canada. Until such time as we have

satisfied the needs of our own people we should not turn our attention to other markets. We find all nations endeavouring to increase their trade simply because competition is becoming so keen. They are endeavouring to turn their attention to other countries. Why are they doing that? Do they do it because they want to go to other countries and kill? I do not think so. I do not believe Italy went into Ethiopia with only the desire to kill the citizens of that country. I do not believe, when Germany entered the last war, she did so merely for the opportunity of killing. She went to war for a definite purpose, namely to extend her boundaries.
Why did Italy or Germany wish to extend their boundaries? They had that desire because the great nations are becoming overcrowded and because they were searching for further supplies of natural resources. Circumstances compelled them to take such action. They have been compelled through circumstances which we, ourselves, as a world people, have built up. The whole matter has evolved itself into a European situation, one which, as was stated by the hon. member who just took his seat, in some way or another we must be above.
I do not believe we can sit idly by and permit ourselves to see the policies of other nations drawing us into a web which is eventually going to turn to war. It has been pointed out that in the house we must be cautious as to the remarks we make respecting the policies of other countries. There is a fear that observations might draw us into a serious situation which could develop into war. The European situation, however, has a bearing on the situation right here in Canada.
When we turn for a moment to look into the European situation we find that not very long ago Germany annexed Austria. It is somewhat of a coincidence that not long ago in this city I was speaking to an individual- not the one about whom I spoke a moment ago-who was well versed in foreign affairs. With respect to this question he said to me that the annexation of Austria by Germany should never have been permitted in the manner in which it was accomplished. He claimed that the greatest mistake was made at the conclusion of the last war, and it was his opinion that it was inevitable that Germany should take Austria. He then asked why we should prolong action until a time when Germany was forced to enter Austria and take it in the manner in which she did.
Germany learned a great lesson from the last war. We know how it developed-through transgressing the rights of Belgium. The

invasion of that little country was what caused the entrance of Great Britain. Germany has now learned her lesson. We see that this time she did not attempt annexation in that way, but was content to use another and a more clever device which achieved exactly the same purpose.
Since the last war Germany has grown up to be a tremendous nation, and it has been stated over and over again that she did not have sufficient people to do the work she had outlined. Someone may say, "Oh, yes, but she conscripted all her men for the army." I do not care what she did with them. The fact remains that there were no unemployed. We condemn her methods; but through all the criticism we pass upon Germany it must be clearly remembered and understood that the Germans are an intelligent people, and the very fact that the followers of Hitler are found in such large, numbers is proof that the German people are doing a great deal of thinking. I believe, if the world had taken advantage of the situation before Germany annexed Austria, we would have saved ourselves a great deal of trouble. As I stated last year-and I have not changed my stand in the meantime-I believe there should have been a conference of nations; probably the best results could have
been obtained through the League of Nations, but such conference should have been held. Take the case of the annexation of Ethiopia by Italy. This conference could have been called, and if it could have been shown that Italy needed more territory or access to more raw materials in order to keep up her industrial life, then possibly these matters could have been settled. I do not say that consideration should be given to the need of materials for the manufacture of muntions. This is something to which we shall have to turn our attention sooner or later. We shall have to see that all nations are satisfied as far as their domestic requirements are concerned. Other countries that have natural resources in abundance may possibly have to cooperate. This is one of the things that must eventually come about.
I should like to refer to the invasion of Ethiopia by Italy because it leads up to another point in my argument. I think it is generally conceded that when that occurred most countries objected, but the tables have now been turned. It is rumoured that the British Empire is to concur in that annexation and permit Ethiopia to become part of the Italian empire. I cannot see how Canada will be able to keep out of these things. As the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, when Great Britain goes to war, Canada goes to war whether or not we like it. That is stated definitely in the statutes of Canada. When Great Britain is at war, we are at war. If we are going to be involved in these matters, then I think we should give serious consideration to the manner in which we are going to be drawn into them.
There is another question in which I think Canada should concern itself. Mind you, Mr. Chairman, I am not saying that we should concern ourselves in these matters to the extent that we would be ready to take any part in action that might be taken by other nations. If we are going to participate in these matters, then we have to expect the natural results. There is another situation arising in connection with Czechoslovakia. In my opinion the geographical location of that country is such that it is bound to be taken over by Germany, not in the manner in which Germany attempted to expand in 1914, but in a manner more like the annexation of Austria. Who is there to stop her? No force was used in connection with Austria; it was simply a matter of nazi-izing, if I may use that term, the country. The same thing will occur in Czechoslovakia. That country is going to be taken over whether or not we like it. Russia has guaranteed protection to
Supply-National Defence

Czechoslovakia. France has guaranteed protection to Russia. Great Britain has guaranteed protection to France. Where does Canada come in?
The point I wish to make is this: Is Canada prepared to enter a European war because of Czechoslovakia? Is Canada prepared to enter a war because of a conflict between Ethiopia and Italy? Is Canada prepared to participate in a war between China and Japan? Is she prepared to do these things any more than she would be prepared to go to war with Germany because of the annexation of Czechoslovakia? I think not. That is something about which we should not concern ourselves. As I have said before in this house, I do not think we should interfere with other countries. We should attend solely to our own affairs. I do not say that we should break away from the British Empire; I say that Great Britain should adopt a similar policy. If all the British Empire stayed together, there would be no difficulty. We should adopt the attitude of minding our own business and letting the other fellows do the same. This brings me more or less to the statement made by the hon. member who spoke a while ago, about this government having no commitments. I have in my hand a copy of an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of March 18, 1938, and which reads:
Canada Should Keep Out of War
There is no hint of the Canadian parliament being consulted on Canada's war liabilities before the eleventh hour, but there is every likelihood that the Minister of External Affairs, Premier Mackenzie King, is being informed from day to day by the British authorities at Whitehall. They are, doubtless, anxiously looking for guidance in the task of determining British foreign policy.
A Canadian press dispatch from London yesterday stated that the United Kingdom government is "working in close consultation with the dominion governments in an endeavour to evolve a program to meet the increasingly grave international situation." It may be taken as highly probable that this Canadian press statement is based on information from official sources in London.
The people of Canada, even the representatives of the people in parliament at Ottawa, seem to be in the dark on Canada's position with regard to the situation in Europe. The members are rarely given an opportunity to express themselves on the floor of the house. They are easily discouraged from offering any guidance.
Without being consulted, this parliament sanctioned Premier Mackenzie King's decision to substitute His Royal Highness the Duke of York for Edward VIII as King of Canada. A similar decision to indicate-or to do nothing to indicate-the extent of Canadian cooperation with the United Kingdom in an impending
[Mr. C. E. Johnston.)
European upheaval, without consulting the dominion parliament until after the event, could apparently be made without much protest on the part of members on parliament hill.
Whether or not that is true, I cannot say, but I do not think many hon. members will contend that the press is not telling the truth. If they do not tell the truth, then I take the stand I have always taken, that they should be forced to tell the truth. The evidence is that there is a close contact. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) makes his statement with regard to the policy of this government, as I understand he will do in a day or two, I hope he makes clear the position of Canada. I should like him to state that this dominion will never participate in a foreign war without the consent of the people. There should be the consent of the people, not just the consent of parliament. It might be said that this parliament gave its sanction as far as Edward VIII was concerned, but that was given after the event. I hope the policy of this government will be made perfectly clear when the Prime Minister makes his statement.
I continue with the editorial:
At the same time, British statesmen seem to leave no doubt about the close cooperation of Great Britain with France. It is at this point that Canadian opinion would do well to be clear on Canada's responsibility as a member of the family of British nations.
It goes on to say:
Lord Halifax stated in the House of Lords last Wednesday that Great Britain is anxious to have the dominions as well as the people of the United Kingdom united behind any steps that may be taken to deal with the grave situation in Europe. Lord Halifax is reported as saying that British foreign policy must be conducted "so it may deserve and command support in this country of a united people, and in the dominions of a united empire."
If that statement is true, then it is manifest that Canada is going to take part, whether or not she likes it. It has been said that no commitments have been made, but apparently Great Britain has assumed that we have made commitments. Therefore, we are going to be held responsible. If this is not so, I should like the Prime Minister to make a definite statement in order to counteract the impression that has gone abroad. Apparently this is the opinion of the press and the people of Great Britain, and I think we should be very cautious. Our policy should be one of distinct neutrality. That is a very difficult road to follow. As I have stated before, I think we should have one of the best defended countries in the world, and I make no apology for making that statement. I should like to

Supply-National Defence
see the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) spend more money on defence, although I may tell him quite frankly that I do not like the method by which he raises the money. But I think we should follow a policy of neutrality. Let us see whether we are following such a policy or whether we are making commitments, probably innocently, but nevertheless commitments.
I have a clipping here dated London, England, March 21:
It was learned here to-day that the Chamberlain government's negotiations with Mussolini's representatives for a pact between London and Rome are nearing completion.
Italian troops were reported withdrawing from Libya as a concession to Britain.
The fact that Chamberlain is making a pact with Mussolini is greatly displeasing the public. Yesterday 20,000 people marched through the streets of London protesting such a pact and shouting: "Chamberlain must go!"
This is the part I want the committee to note:
It is understood that the pact includes provisions for a large loan to the Italian dictator, whose country is near to a financial crisis.
If that loan is negotiated, will there not be a commitment? Will not everyone who subscribes to the loan be more or less involved in the outcome? I say that you are automatically committing yourself there, whether you like it or not.
We had a good many statements not long ago about a boycott; but the very fact that you boycott a nation means that you are taking sides. There again you are definitely committing yourself, whether you like it or not. Some persons suggested that we should send munitions to the loyalists in Spain to even things up. That may be all right, but as soon as you do that you are making commitments. That is not leading to the road of neutrality. You must be consistent. If you are going to keep out of these troubles, you must keep out of them entirely, and let these other nations work out their own affairs. All these things tend to develop a public opinion; whether intentionally or unintentionally is not the point; the fact is that they do develop public opinion.
There is one other thing which makes it exceedingly difficult for us to stay neutral, and that is the exportation of arms and munitions from this country. I hold in my hand sessional paper No. 204, which I asked for in the house some time ago. It shows the number of permits issued and the value of our exports of arms and ammunition. This was the answer that was brought down:
196 permits were issued from July 31, 1937, to date-
That would be about nine months:
-for the exportation of arms, ammunition, implements or munitions of war.
That is an average of twenty-four permits a month. How can we stay neutral under those circumstances?

I will show you in a moment why not. Permits were issued to the number of thirty-four for the export of a total value of arms and ammunition to the United Kingdom of $233595.83; to Australia, the total value of the shipments was $11,052.03, and the number of permits issued, twenty; Newfoundland, total value of shipments, $5,316.19, and fifteen permits issued; New Guinea, total value of shipments, $2,890, and one permit issued; New Zealand, total value of shipments, S5,000, and one permit 'issued; Trinidad, total value, $9.98, and one permit issued; the Argentine, total value, $90,336, and five permits issued; Brazil, total value, $550, and one permit issued; China, total value, $210500, and thirty-five permits issued. We have shipped directly to China, a nation at war, arms and ammunition to help that country. Is that neutrality? I cannot conceive that to be neutrality because you are definitely taking sides. To the Dominican Republic we shipped arms and ammunition to a total value of $16,168, and one permit issued; Japan, total value of shipments, $43,500, and two permits issued. We shipped that amount of war materials to Japan. We are supplying both China and Japan with munitions. Is that taking the road to neutrality? Surely that is not a neutral stand we are taking. I think it is one of the most definite commitments we could make, and yet we are endeavouring to take a neutral stand. To Nicaragua we shipped arms and ammunition to a total value of $40,600, and two permits issued; Norway, total value of shipments $84, and one permit issued; Turkey, total value of shipments, $266,892.20, and three permits issued. To the United States, which is one of the best equipped nations in the world to manufacture arms and munitions of war, we shipped $59,134.46 worth of arms and ammunition, and sixty-nine permits were issued. I wonder where those munitions went after they were shipped to the United States. No doubt they went to Italy, China, Japan, or some other of the warring nations. Altogether we shipped arms and munitions to a total value of $1,051,781.69, and the total number of permits issued was 196. Those were munitions all ready for use; the figures do not include raw materials.

I have in my hand, another return, which I shall not read in detail, but it shows the amount of scrap iron or steel, aluminum scrap, brass scrap, nickel and copper that we shipped out of this country between 1935 and 1937. Let me give the figures for nickel. In 1935 we shipped out of this country 1,427,265 hundredweight of nickel, of a total value of $36,285,482; in 1936, 1,736,375 hundredweight, of a total value of $44,594,296; in 1937, 2,227,700 hundredweight, of a total value of $58,913,217. And we are taking a neutral stand! Think of the tremendous amount of war material we have shipped to these warring countries, and yet we are endeavouring to be neutral! We say we have made no commitments. It seems to me that our commitments could not be greater or more offensive to other nations than the very ones we have made in this way.
Here is another article headed, ''Canadian delegate states Canada is arsenal of Japan." It reads in part:
On Saturday the Canadian delegate declared that "Canada is the arsenal of Japan; but for war materials from Canada it would have been impossible for Japan to begin her aggression and impossible for her to continue it."
Addressing 900 delegates from 19 countries, Mr. MacLeod declared that in 1936 Canada supplied Japan with 71-7 per cent of its aluminum for aircraft; 79-11 per cent of her copper and, directly or indirectly, 100 per cent of her nickel.
"Any movement against Japanese aggression which does not lead to a government embargo on shipments of war material," he said, "would be absolutely meaningless."
I stated last year that I thought it was the government's duty to declare an embargo on shipments of war material, and I still think that is the proper course for it to take. Last year, when speaking on this question, the Prime Minister informed me that an investigation was being made into the manufacture of munitions to find out if any profiteering was going on. I have not heard of any report being made on that investigation. I think it was the proper course to inquire into the matter, and I think the report should be made public if there was an investigation, so that the public would know whether there was any profiteering or not in that industry. I have never contended that our manufacturers should make munitions for nothing; I think they should have a reasonable commission, and no one, I think, would contend to the contrary; but when it comes to profiteering I think that is wrong. When we ship arms and munitions to countries that are openly engaged in war, I think it is absolutely wrong and is leading us right into war, and I believe we should

declare our policy most emphatically when the Prime Minister is making his statement on foreign policy.
I have no objection to defence; I believe we should be properly defended, and I think the suggestion made by an hon. member a short while ago in regard to the defence of our coasts is sound. He is an army man and knows better than some of the rest of us do what the requirements are, and no doubt the minister will avail himself of the information which that hon. gentleman has given. I would suggest, however, that defence divides itself into two parts. In the first place, provision must be made for weapons-airplanes, machine guns and things of that sort. And let me say that, if the need arises, we can build those things right here in Canada. For that matter, we could start now. We have an admirable beginning in our aircraft. But one of the greatest forms of defence, one form that we are neglecting, the one most essential, is the proper care of our people, because when war is declared you must have healthy men to fight. And how will you have healthy men unless you pay attention to them now? You will not have good, healthy men in the ranks of the unemployed if you leave them poorly clad and housed and ill fed. One of the main considerations of the government should be to see that our people are properly cared for. That was what they promised in 1935, and that is what they should be giving their attention to at the present time.
But the question will be asked, Where is the money to come from? I said a moment ago that I did not agree with the government's plan of raising money for defence. Let me repeat, I have no objection to defence, but I must vote against this estimate for the same reason that I gave last year: I object to the method by which the money is to be raised. The Prime Minister in 1935 said that he would issue money in terms of public need. Surely there is no greater public need than the defence of the country. And there is no greater need in times of peace than the proper care of the citizens of the country. If the Prime Minister would put that promise into effect, I would have no objection to this estimate. If he would issue debt-free money to take care of defence, instead of piling up the national debt by increasing taxation; if he would devise a plan of that sort and issue money in terms of public need, debt free, then there would not be anyone who would vote against these estimates. We must have more money if we are to have defence; and where will it come

from? The Minister of Labour on March 2, as reported at page 979 of Hansard, made a statement from which I wish to quote:
.	.	. but the dominion government can appeal to no one for grants in aid. In connection with its increased expenditures it can go only to the taxpayers of this country. That is a consideration which we are bound to keep in view.
That, it seems, is where the money is to come from. Further on, he said:
I think it is quite clear from the returns made by the income tax branch of the Department of National Revenue that it would be quite impossible to raise this additional sum by increasing the taxes imposed on the higher brackets of income.
Rest assured it will not come from the higher brackets.
No doubt some additional income could be obtained in that way-so far as I am concerned I would prefer that it be done in that manner- but there is no doubt that if we endeavoured to obtain this revenue it would be necessary to go into the lower brackets of income where we would be taxing once more the small home owners who have already been seriously affected by the heavy burden of relief in our municipalities.
If we have to build up a defence force by means of money obtained from that source, then I say that we are destroying the greatest arm of defence that we have-the health and well-being of our citizens who must necessarily participate in any war of defence. On the next page the minister is reported as follows:
If we did not have recourse to the income tax to raise the money required by the dominion government taking over the entire cost of relief, we would have to consider the sales tax. I think it will be agreed that here again we would be burdening that group of moderate wage earners who represent, so to speak, the working force of the country as a whole. Not only that, but with an increase in the sales tax we would be providing another deterrent to a revival of the building industry.
It is clear from the foregoing exactly how the government intends to get the money to build up a defence force. Perhaps, however, I am wrong, because the Minister of National Defence did say that he would issue $500,000,000. I hope he will persuade the government to do this. If he does, I can assure him that I shall vote for this estimate. I hope that he will carry out that promise which he made in the west.
